p.t: In short
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t:
Pick a product that fits the **season** in the country you sell to.
Launch **well before** the season or holiday. For Christmas, aim for **late October**.

If a holiday is only **2 to 3 weeks** away, it is usually too late. Pick the next one.
**Choose the country first**, then judge the product.
**Test where the product is not yet crowded**, because competition and ad costs are lower there.
Use a **VPN** (a tool that makes your internet look like it comes from another country) set to the target country. Then search results show what local buyers see.

Check **demand, competition and shipping** before you spend money on ads or stock.
**Test a proven product** in a new language or country before you build a full store.
Avoid products with waits of **about 10 weeks or more**, and products sold out for months.
Season and timing principles
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: A product must match the season that is **active** in the target market (the country or group of buyers you sell to).

A cold-weather product should not run in hot summer months.
Seasonal timing matters **more than most beginners expect**.
The same offer (the product plus its price and deal) can **fail in one month and succeed in another**.
A winter product that did not sell in April started selling in **November**, when the weather turned cold.
A product that did poorly in August or September can be **retried in November** (Q4, the last three months of the year: October to December).

It may perform better the second time.
Seasonal products sell most when **launched well before the event**.

Early sellers capture most of the demand.
For Christmas products, the recommended timing is a launch in **late October**, on Halloween or on the day after.
Seasonal products can be copied quickly.
A supplier (the factory or company that makes and ships your product) can have shipping times that delay your launch.

Prepare the **next seasonal product as early as possible** to avoid competing with copycats (sellers who copy your product).
Seasonal ideas need **early timing**.

A trend from last year, such as a holiday costume trend, is usually too late once the season has started.
List seasonal products **well before the peak**.

Seasonal products can be planned **months ahead**.
Check whether competitors already post content for the season.
Search older seasonal terms to see whether demand existed in past years.
Use Google Trends (a free Google tool that shows search interest over time) to **confirm a spike** (a sudden jump in interest) before testing.

Check the trend for the product itself, **not only its category**.
**Test seasonal ideas before the season begins.**
For a summer product, prepare the offer **several weeks before** the season starts.
Season and timing principles (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: Time the test of cooling or ice-based products ahead of the warm season, so the test runs while buying interest is **rising**.

A product tested out of season may show weak sales that do not reflect its real potential.
Time the launch to the **start of the season** in the target market.
The speaker launched a summer-type product in Australia around **September**, when the weather there turned warm.

Seasonal products must launch in their **peak window** (the time when demand is highest).
An ice cream product tested late in summer converted poorly (few visitors bought).

Early summer (about **May to June**) is the better launch window.
Timing can matter **more than the ad itself**.
A pen product made about **30,000 USD** in one month (August) with about 6 million views.

It matched back-to-school demand (buying for the new school year).
Start research by identifying **problems or needs** people have in a specific period.

Then look for trending products that solve them.
Do not hunt for winning products **at random**.
Before a Q4 push (extra sales effort in the last quarter), choose a product **unique enough to stand out** in a crowded marketplace (a shop platform where many sellers sell).
An example is a product that solves a problem differently from common alternatives.
Products that are **not yet saturated** (not yet sold by too many sellers) in January and February often have low CPC (cost per click: what you pay for one click on an ad).
Low CPC happens because there is less competition for ad space (the spots where ads appear).
If you find a working product before that period, **buy stock early** (stock is the goods you hold).

Factories may close during Chinese New Year (a major holiday in China).
Seasonal products such as kids' toys can be **tested before Q4 and Christmas**.
Start searching early enough to have stock and ads ready **before demand peaks**.

p.t:

Note: High-opportunity period

Window: Launch late October, on Halloween or the day after

Note: Recommended launch timing

Note: Late-summer test converted poorly

Window: August

Note: Out-of-season tests understate potential

Window: March to August or September

Window: Q4 (October to December), around Black Friday (the big US shopping day after Thanksgiving) and Christmas
Note: Time the test to the peak

Window: Q1 (January to March), New Year's resolutions
Note: Fitness products worth testing in Q1

Window: End of Q4 and start of the new year
Note: Seasonal demand

**Home fitness and outdoor fitness**
Window: Expected to rise in January
Note: New Year resolutions

Window: Summer
Note: Prepare the offer several weeks before the season

Window: Campaigns from late November or mid-December
Note: Pre-test content (test ads and content before launch) 2 months before the event
Q4 and gift products
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: Products that peak in Q4 (October through December) include gadgets, jewelry, kids' items, dog and pet products, fashion items,

customizable gifts, toys and baby products.
Gift products sell **especially well**.
Customers buy for others, not only for themselves.

Gift niches that performed strongest in Q4 were kids toys, personalized jewelry and winter clothing.
Christmas gifting drives this demand.
Winners in Q4 included children's gifts, winter clothing, and winter shoes that keep feet warm.

Personalized jewelry, such as name or message pieces, also won in Q4.
These categories are **not to be copied exactly**.

Use them as a basis for product research.
Personalized gifts and gifts for parents, kids or grandchildren sell well around Christmas and in Q4.
Kids toys were also a Q4 product for the seller in this example.

Gift products such as personalized necklaces, and gifts for parents or kids, suit Christmas.
Non-electronic gifts are preferred over electronics.

They carry less customs risk (border checks and import fees on goods) and less quality risk.
Children's toys work well in Q4.
Giftable products tend to perform strongly in winter.

Shipping times must be **reliable**.
Late delivery is a serious risk around gift periods.
Seasonal winners in Q4 2024 included:
hoodies that began in **five** simple colors and later grew into many designs;
family matching clothing for kids, babies and adults in the winter, when energy prices were high;
games, toys and puzzles, which also performed well in Q4 when people stayed at home during lockdowns (times when people were ordered to stay home).
Health supplements show **strong Q4 demand** around Black Friday and Christmas.
Climate and weather-linked products
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: Fashion and seasonal apparel (clothing) align with climate shifts.

**Push** sweaters and cold-weather items in fall and winter.
Push them then because customers actually need them.

Look for products that solve a seasonal or environmental problem in the target market.
In Switzerland, summer runs roughly from **May to the end of September**.
So cold-weather products have demand during the rest of the year.
Energy shortage concerns (fears of not having enough power and heat) in Europe from 2022 onward made warmth a stronger need.

That supported a cold-weather product.
Watch current events that affect how people heat or warm their homes.

(Dated: this reflects the 2022 situation.)
Climate-related products sell **better where the cold is extreme**.
Sweden at minus 20 degrees compares with Switzerland at minus 4 degrees.
Check where the use case (the situation where people use the product) is strongest **before choosing the test market**.
Warm-weather products such as summer outfits or swimwear should be tested in warm markets such as the US or Australia.

Test them there **rather than Europe at the start of the year**.
Cold-weather products, such as winter items, can be tested in **every market**.
A season-tied product, such as golf scratch repair in winter, may have **low demand at certain times**.
Cold and rainy weather in Europe can make a warming or comfort product relevant.
Climate and weather-linked products (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t:
In cold months in Europe and the US, products that fit the weather and winter gifting can be tested.
Examples are heated tea cups or tea warmers.

Choose products by **what fits the current season** in the target country.
Do not choose only by what a spy tool shows (a tool that shows what other sellers sell).
Tool-type products that solve a practical home problem may work best in Australia, the US and Canada.
Weather-related products, such as summer dresses, should be tested in countries where the season is **only starting**.

Use a seasonal angle (a theme tied to the season), such as a pre-summer sale.
Relaunch a seasonal niche **ahead of its demand peak**.

For home decor in Switzerland, the spring cleaning season starts about **one month before the relaunch**.
Cold, snowy months showed little interest.

Weather-linked and seasonal products can be good niches.
Examples are cooling products for summer and warm or pet protection products for winter.
Niches such as camping and adventure perform well when targeting Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the US.

Sub-niches (smaller parts of a niche) with passionate audiences also work well.
They make audience targeting (choosing who sees your ads) clearer.

Seasonal product example: Apple Watch straps are a **summer product**.
People walk and do outdoor activities more in summer, and they use the watch more.
Heat-friendly fabric and bright colors help.
In the test, TikTok ads (ads shown in the TikTok app) cost **less per acquisition** (per new customer bought) than Facebook ads.
A free wallpaper or theme download was used as an **add-on offer** (a free extra given with the purchase).
Hemisphere shifts (north and south halves of the earth) and extending a season
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: A seasonal product can be extended by switching to a market in the **opposite**

**hemisphere**.
For example, a winter product can be sold to US buyers in winter while the Australian audience is in summer.

This keeps sales going **after the home-market season ends**.
Seasonal products sell well **only in their season**.
So a seasonal brand needs extra tactics and new markets in the off-season (the time when the season is over).

Testing winter products in Australia while it is summer in Europe can keep sales going.
Seasons are **reversed** in the Southern Hemisphere.
A product that sold well in the Northern winter can be tested in Southern winter markets such as Australia.

Summer products that worked in the Northern hemisphere can be tested there during the Southern summer.
Winter products depend on hemisphere.

It is summer in the southern hemisphere while it is winter in the north.
So check the target market **before choosing seasonal items**.
Seasonal niches can be tested by checking what sells in one hemisphere's season for the other market.

For example, winter products in the US can be tested in Australia during its winter.
Searching for a product in the US and selling it in another market is a **valid test method**.
Products that did well in summer can be tested in Australia, where summer starts when the Northern Hemisphere is in winter.
Products that sold well in Australian summer can be tested in Europe or the US during winter.
Products that worked in the northern summer can be tested in Australia, which enters summer in Q4.
Holiday and event launch deadlines
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: A holiday is only worth targeting if there is **time to prepare and run ads** before it.

If the holiday is only **two to three weeks away**, it is generally too late.
Choose the next upcoming event instead.

Avoid testing a product with a **very close deadline**.
Example: Halloween, when it is only a day away.
Products for a holiday need to be tested **well ahead of time**.

Launch windows and deadlines differ by step, not by contradiction.
The Christmas launch window is **late October through Halloween or the day after**.

A product with a deadline one day away should **not be tested**.
Seasonal products such as Valentine's Day and Mother's Day can be sold.
But orders must be **delivered before the date** to avoid chargebacks (when a bank takes money back after a customer disputes an order).
The presenter avoids fixed-date products (products tied to one set date) because of delivery risk and Chinese New Year timing.

Q4 gift products should be **tested early enough to arrive before Christmas**.
Establish the **last date** an order can be shipped and still arrive on time.
For a Valentine's Day campaign, **pre-test content 2 months before** the event.
For gift products that overlap with Christmas, such as love bracelets and charm jewelry, use the same products and content.
Adjust the messaging (the words used in ads and on the store) **2 weeks before each occasion**.

For a Valentine's Day campaign, the store is built about **one month before** the holiday.
The winning product should be found at least about **15 days before** the holiday.
Choosing the target market
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: The same niche (a narrow group of buyers and their product area) can be approved in one country and rejected in another.

This happens because competitor and supplier targets differ per market.
Set the **target country before grading any niche**.
When researching **high-ticket dropshipping** (selling expensive products that a supplier ships directly to the buyer), choose the market to sell into first.

Then select the specific products within that market.
This keeps product ideas tied to a market that can support them.
Infer the target country from the competitor store.
A store in US dollars and English is assumed to target the **US**.
Traffic-estimation tools (tools that guess how many visitors a site gets) were unreliable in the mentor's own checks.

Trust their country data **only when it points overwhelmingly to one country**.
Competitors running ads for the same product usually target the same **top four or five countries**.

Use that cluster as the starting market list for a new test.
Expand to other markets **only after the first data comes in**.
Most dropshippers in these examples target the top markets of the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand.
Products that target the US, Australia and Canada were treated as the main markets to evaluate.
Starting countries for first testing: the US, Canada, Australia and the UK are the **strongest**.
They are English-speaking, accept credit cards and PayPal (an online payment service), and have good online buying habits.
Conflict note: this is the default for English-speaking tests.
When CPM (the ad cost per 1,000 views) in these markets is **too high**, the European choice applies instead; see the competition section.
The Big Five markets (USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) are the **usual default**.

Smaller markets such as Greece are weaker because of lower buying power and higher shipping cost.
That makes dropshipping harder there.
Choosing the target market (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t:
Simple pages may convert more easily there.
Targeting options for initial tests: the US, the UK or Australia.
Or a native-language market (a country whose main language you speak), such as Germany or France, if the operator speaks that language.
Test first in a market whose language you speak and whose buying habits you understand, such as your home country.

There is usually **less competition** from dropshippers there.
Once you have results, you can expand.

You do not have to stay in that country.
Germany, Switzerland and Austria can offer lower competition for many products.

They also have strong buying power (how much money buyers can spend).
Test them when capacity allows (when you have the time and money).
When a shortlist (a short selected list) is built for one home market, only test products that suit that country's buyers.
A list of 5 to 10 products may yield only **two or three** candidates for a single market such as Switzerland.
For a trend-based approach, find products trending in the US or Canada over the **last two months**.
Then test them in smaller markets such as Australia, New Zealand, Germany and Switzerland.
Pick products that could sell in German-speaking and English-speaking markets, such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Australia.
Build a separate store branding (the store's name, look and identity) and language for each market.

The ideal product idea is one that is **already selling well** in another market and can be brought to a new one.
Find the **problem first**, then the solution.

Sending a product to multiple countries may reveal different results.
A product that failed in one market can work in another.
Consider countries with e-commerce potential (room to grow in online buying and selling) beyond the usual German-speaking markets, and test them.

Start in the country where you speak the language well.
For an English speaker, that is the **US**.
Choosing the target market (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t:
Starting in a country with a language barrier adds work at the beginning.
France was one of the first markets where shoppers encountered dropshipping.
So French buyers easily recognize generic dropshipping stores (plain stores that look like many others).
A French launch needs **custom content and full native translation** (a translation that reads as if a native speaker wrote it).

It still requires research into local brands and trust.
In the EU, fashion is presented as a strong niche for general stores, especially in France.

In France, fashion and orthopedic sneakers (shoes designed for foot support) sell well.
Beauty products also perform well in France.

Test products through **pricing and messaging** in a single market first.
Expand to other countries **once the audience is clear**.

Competition, CPM and market-size checks
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: Check market competition in each country **before choosing it**.
Alternative markets such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria, the Scandinavian countries, France and Belgium were recommended.

They were recommended **over the US and Canada**, where ad costs are high.
Canada, Australia and the US were described as **expensive for testing** in recent periods.

This pushed the choice toward European markets.
Check current CPM in each country **before choosing a test market**.
A store focused only on Canada usually faces **less competition** than a store primarily targeting the US market.

The same logic applies to other English-speaking markets such as Australia or the UK.
Products trending in the US can be sold in other markets, where competition is **lower**.

A US trend tested on TikTok produced **weaker results than expected**.
Choose products that are trending in the United States.

Sell them in other markets such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Australia, New Zealand or Canada.
Competition there is lower.

The combined German-speaking market (Germany, Switzerland, Austria) is about **100 million** people.
Saturation in the US does **not rule out** a product.
Being an early adopter (the first seller in a new market) with a better offer can still produce strong results.

This works even if many advertisers run the same product in the US.
Avoid launching a product in the United States when it is **already heavily sold** there.

Saturation makes it hard to win.
Test instead in markets where the same product is not yet common, such as Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Switzerland or Austria.

Products already advertised heavily in one market are **proof of demand**.
So they are a good starting point for research.

Take such a product and test it in a different market where competition is lower.
An ad running in only one country tells you that the product may already sell there.

It does **not** tell you that the product will fail elsewhere.
A product with strong engagement (likes, comments and shares) in one market can be tested in another.

A product that is saturated in the US, which has high CPMs, can still be a valid candidate.
This applies when it is moved to a cheaper market.
Competition, CPM and market-size checks (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t:
In a cheaper market, competition is often lower and ads cost less.
Test the transferred product in the new market **before judging it**.
Target countries where the product is in season and CPMs are lower.
For seasonal holidays such as Halloween, consider other countries with lower CPM if the US CPM is **too high**.
Halloween is celebrated in many countries, not only the US.

For seasonal demand such as Halloween, sell in countries where CPM is lower if the US CPM is **too high**.
Niche criteria must be adjusted to the market size.
The US demand numbers are not comparable with Canada because of population differences (2024).
Countries with small populations, such as Canada, do not work with the **same niche criteria** as the US.

Use revised criteria for smaller markets instead of applying US thresholds (minimum numbers a niche must reach).
(2024)
For a demand test in a smaller country, a population share can justify a **lower target**.

If the UK has about 20 percent of the US population, either find a bigger niche or move one level broader.
Do **not** lower the target blindly. -

The US niche validation uses a **demand threshold of 10,000**.
Smaller markets such as Australia have fewer sub-niches (smaller parts of a niche).
So sellers there may need to **niche up a level** (move to a broader category) to reach that threshold.
Niches selling to a small population should be widened to a broader category so enough visitors arrive.

Large-population markets can use very specific niche stores, which convert better.
Pandemic conditions in 2020 did **not change** the product selection criteria.

Recession (an economic downturn) or fear-driven concerns should not be used to drop a niche that passes the tests.
Online buying remained strong.
Research steps for a new country
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: 1. **Set a VPN** (a tool that makes your internet look like it comes from another country) to the target country.
Then search the supplier name or product on Google Shopping (Google's product search) to see local results.
2. Use the **Source A research tool** (a tool that shows how often people search for a product) with the target country selected. Check whether people search for the product there.
3. Search results depend on location. When you research a market in a country where you do not live, use a VPN and **set the location to the country you plan to sell in**.
Otherwise, results may come from your home country or other countries.
4. Use a VPN set to the target country so **Google returns local results**.
Without it, search results from another country distort findings about competitors (sellers who sell the same kind of thing) and niches (small groups of buyers with one shared interest).
5. Market size check using the **Facebook Ad Library** (Meta's public list of all ads running on Facebook and Instagram):
1. Search for the outlook for growth or **market valuation** (the estimated total money value of the market) of the industry (for example the pet industry).
2. Check the ad library for each target country (for example Germany) to see how many sellers run ads there.
3. Countries with lower **saturation** (how crowded a market is with sellers) are better **test markets** (countries where you try a product on a small budget first).
6. Facebook Ad Library country check:
1. Search a product keyword in the Facebook Ad Library. Use the **country filter** (a setting that shows one country only) to limit results to one market, such as the United States.
2. Compare it with a test market such as Germany. Low **scaling** (spending more on ads that already sell) in the test market suggests room for a new seller.

7. **Check whether a product is popular** in each target country before testing. A product that sells well in one country may not sell in another. For example, air fryers are less common in Switzerland than in the US.
8. Compare the new country's shipping systems (the roads, carriers and warehouses that move parcels) and **supplier responsiveness** (how fast suppliers answer) with a market you already know.
Check how quickly suppliers reply and how reliably parcels arrive before you commit money to ads or inventory (the goods you hold in stock).
Language, translation and language arbitrage
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: **Test products in English-speaking markets** before translating the store into other languages.
Do this even if competitors are not marketing there.
Translation needs two things: professional translation services, and a customer service **virtual assistant** (a remote helper who answers customers) who speaks that language fluently.
Together, these add significant cost and complexity.
Start product research with English-language ads. The US English market has a larger **total addressable market (TAM)** (all the buyers you could reach) than smaller language markets.
Study which creatives (ad images and videos) and messages already run there before you look at **underserved markets** (markets few sellers serve).
**Language arbitrage** (profiting from a language gap): take an ad that already **converts** (turns viewers into buyers) in one language and **run it in a language market that has not seen it yet**.
The Spanish-speaking market in the US has about 60 million people. Its TAM is smaller than the English market, but it has far less competition.
The Spanish-language market in the US is **largely untapped** (few sellers serve it yet). Its TAM is smaller than the white and Black American markets.
But **ad auctions** (the bidding for ad space) are less crowded, so demand is proven while competition is not.
Products whose ads are mostly in Spanish can be run. But **only run them if** the landing pages (the page buyers arrive on after clicking) are customized and everything is translated into Spanish.
This is harder for a beginner, so **beginners should skip Spanish-language ad products** at the start.
Taobao videos (videos from Taobao, a large Chinese shopping site) mostly feature Asian presenters and may underperform in the US market.
**Recast them** (replace the people on screen) with white or Black American talent when you produce custom ads for the US.
When the market is English-speaking, a product that worked for a long time there can be tested in other languages such as German or French.
Language, translation and language arbitrage (continued)
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: Native-language markets (countries where that language is the everyday language) often have less competition.
**Validate** a product that sells well in one country. Run the same product with ads in the language of another target market.

If the new market also shows a strong **hook rate** (the share of viewers who keep watching past the first seconds) and **CTR** (click-through rate: the share of viewers who click), the product is worth more store work.

When testing an **ebook** (a digital book) or another digital product in a new country, **translate the mockup** (a rough preview of the product) and the **ad copy** (the written words in the ad) into that country's language before
you run ads. The example built a German mockup for a German market test. This makes it possible to judge whether the offer itself is attractive to local buyers.
Entering an untapped market needs only minimal effort beyond the product. **Native translations and local payment methods are required.**
**Stripe** (a payment provider) lets you enable the most used payment methods for each country.
**Custom branding** (your own logo and look) or **UGC** (user-generated content: real customer videos and photos) is not needed from the start.
Study what works in other markets to find message patterns (wording that sells again and again). But **do not copy a competitor's exact wording**. Adapt the underlying structure to your own market.
Pricing differs by market. Australian dollars look cheap to US buyers, so **check pricing and currency per country**.
When pricing in countries where the local currency is much smaller than USD (US dollars), such as Malaysia at 4 MYR (Malaysian ringgit) to 1 USD,
**do not automatically adjust price points by converting wholesale cost** (what you pay the supplier). **Validate your intended prices** against what other online stores in that country sell for.
Use **market-based pricing** (prices set by what the local market pays).
For an Italian-market test in Q4 (October to December), classic, mid-priced jewelry was suggested. The reason given was that Italian buyers were said to prefer classic styles over expensive fashion.
**Treat this as a hypothesis** (a guess to test, not a proven fact). Validate it with a small test budget before scaling.
Testing a proven product in a new market
p.s: Seasonality, timing and market selection by country

p.t: **Do not reinvent the wheel.** Take a product that sells well in one market.
Test it in a market where nobody is selling it in volume (in large amounts). Check the product in the new market before scaling.
**Start by testing** products that already show scaling ads in the USA or Australia. A product that works there may also work in other countries.
Adapt the store to the new market, including language and payment methods.
Differentiating by market: **launch a product proven in the US** in English-speaking countries such as Australia, New Zealand, the UK and Canada.
Or launch it in European markets such as Germany, France, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Check in the Facebook Ad Library whether the product is scaling in the new market.
Low competition there is the differentiator (the thing that sets you apart).
Comfy case: a sleeved blanket (a blanket with sleeves), first sold in the US market, was adapted with minor product and design changes.
It was launched in Australia and New Zealand and reached **over 300 million dollars in sales**. The same concept was later launched in Switzerland under a different brand name by another seller.
That seller knew the market well and sold well there.
Question for research into a new product market: if a product is not selling in a new country, check three things. Do competitors exist there? Are their store and ads good?
Does the market accept this product type? A lack of sales usually comes from missing trust, missing native-language content, or the market not yet knowing the product.
The last one requires **educating customers** (teaching buyers what the product is).
Competitor products proven in one market can be tested in another. **Copy the product and store** and change the store currency (for example to euros or Australian dollars) and the language.
Stores in weak condition with many ads running still prove the product sells, so the offer and store can be improved.
Example Swiss test: an early **dropshipping** (selling products that a supplier ships to the buyer, so you hold no stock) test in Switzerland spent about 200 to 300 USD on ads.
Testing a proven product in a new market (continued)

p.h: Supply chain, lead times and delivery

p.t: continents, for example Australia to Europe) makes costs too high. With shipping included, it roughly doubles product prices.
Products that are **backordered** (sold out, waiting for new stock) for months **should not get paid traffic** (visitors from paid ads) until stock returns.
Genuinely custom **made-to-order** products (made only after an order comes in), with a known build time (for example custom pool tables taking about two months), can still be advertised.
Products with production or delivery times of **about 10 weeks or more** should get very limited ad spend (money put into ads).
Customers rarely buy them without knowing the **lead time** (the wait from order to delivery). So the **conversion rate** (the share of visitors who buy) tends to be very low.

Fitness products suffered the most from **port backlogs** (ships waiting to unload at ports) and supplier shortages after 2020. In the 2021 situation, **the fitness industry was the niche to avoid** for the time being.
Stock was thin, and a store could not reliably fill orders.
A weak **supply chain** (the chain of suppliers and shipping that gets products to buyers) can make an otherwise promising niche unworkable.
**Check supplier responsiveness and parcel reliability** before committing money.
Seasonal products (sold only at certain times of year) may be copied quickly. Shipping times from suppliers can delay launches. **Plan the next seasonal product early**.
